BACKGROUND: Although hematoma enlargement and sec-
ondary tissue compression produces early deterioration after ICH,
extent of brain edema also appears to be an important factor
leading to early neurologic compromise. An improved understand-
ing of the evolution of ICH induced edema may be beneficial in
determining the optimal time for intervention.
DESIGN/METHODS: A retrospective MRI volumetric analy-
sis of non-traumatic ICH patients using white matter T2WI hy-
perintensity as surrogate marker of vasogenic edema peripheral
to the hematoma mass was performed. Volume measurements of
blood clots at different stages were performed according to their
specific MRI signal appearance. After determining the degree of
correlation between edema and hematoma volumes, edema vol-
ume/hematoma volume ratios (EV/HV), designed to convey the
evolving edema to hemorrhage volume ratio and to reduce inter-
subject variability, were obtained in each case. We analyzed the
early evolution of EV/HV ratios after ICH in the study cohort.
RESULTS: We identified 28 ICH patients studied with con-
ventional MRI sequences. Mean age of the study cohort was 54.9
(range 15 — 75; SD + 13.2) years. Male/female ratio was 1.3.
Etiology of ICH was hypertension (71.4%), vascular malformation
(17%) and coagulopathy (7.4%). Mean time from symptom onset to
MRI was 11.3 (range 1 — 71; SD + 15.7) days. ICH location was
basal ganglia/thalamic in 34.3%, lobar in 53.6% and cerebellar in
7.1%. IVH was seen in 21.4%. High degree of correlation was
found between EV and HV for the entire cohort (Spearman’s rank
correlation coefficient rho: 0.8, p < 0.001). EV/HV ratio at day 1
was 0.9 (n = 4; range 0.3 - 1.1; SD + 0.4); 2.34 at 2 days (n = 2),
2.5 (n = 4; range 1.5 — 3.3; SD = 0.8) at 3 days, p = 0.01; 3.1 (n =
8; range 0.6 — 9.8; SD + 3.1) at days 4 and 6; and 0.8 (n = 12;
range 0.4 — 1.4; SD = 0.4) after 9 days, p < 0.001.
CONCLUSIONS: Significant increment in edema volume rel-
ative to hematoma mass appears to occur within the first 48 hrs
(and perhaps as early as within 24 hrs) after ICH. If prospectively
confirmed, our observations suggest that any treatment aimed to
prevent/reduce brain edema should be instituted within the initial
48 hrs after ICH, since edema volume expansion could contribute
to early neurologic deterioration after ICH.

Fellowship for Clinical Research Award from the American Philo-
sophical Society. Dr. Beauchamp is supported by a grant from the
American Roentgen Ray Society
PO5.119
Prescribing Practices of Antihypertensive
Agents in Patients with Ischemic Stroke:
Impact on Patient Outcome
Denise H. Rhoney, Karen J. McAllen, Kellie R. Murry, William M.
Coplin, Detroit, MI
OBJECTIVE: To determine if specific classes of antihyperten-
sive agents would result in better control of blood pressure (BP)
with improved patient outcome and decrease length of hospital-
ization in both the acute and chronic period following ischemic
stroke (IS). Secondarily, evaluate the BP treatment threshold
compared to the recommendations of the Stroke Council of the
American Heart Association (AHA) and the percentage reduction
from baseline of the antihypertensives utilized.
BACKGROUND: Antihypertensive treatment of acute IS pa-
tients is generally reserved for those with markedly elevated BP
unless the patient is a candidate for thrombolysis or if concomi-

tant medical conditions are present. It has been recommended by
the AHA to withhold treatment in non-thrombolytic candidates
unless systolic BP (SBP)>220mmHg or mean arterial pressure
(MAP)>130mmHg. We sought to evaluate antihypertensive pre-
scribing practices in our institution.
DESIGN/METHODS: A convenience cohort of patients admit-
ted with the diagnosis of IS to an urban center from 1997-1998
was selected. Variables assessed were: demographics, BP, BP
medications, length of hospitalization, hospital complications, and
patient outcome and disposition. Statistical analysis included de-
scriptives, ANOVA, and Fisher exact test. A P<0.05 was consid-
ered statistically significant.
RESULTS: A total of 61 patients were included in this cohort.
The population was 64% female with a mean age of 66.3 years.
Baseline SBP and MAP were 174%32.4 and 123+18.6mmHg, re-
spectively. None of the patients received thrombolysis or short-
acting nifedipine. Median intensive care unit and hospital lengths
of stay were 4 and 5.5 days respectively. The most commonly
prescribed agents were dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
(DHPCCB) 43% (i.e., amlodipine, extended-release nifedipine),
angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI) 36%, and
clonidine 21%. For breakthrough therapy both clonidine (31%)
and labetalol (21%) were most often used. The largest mean MAP
percent change from baseline during the acute treatment period
was experienced with clonidine (-26%), oral hydralazine (-24%),
oral labetalo] (-24%), intravenous hydralazine (-21%), and nitro-
prusside (-20%). The agent selected did not have a significant
effect on patient outcome or length of hospitalization. 78% of the
cohort received antihypertensive therapy acutely outside the AHA
recommendations. Of these patients, there was a trend towards
worse outcome in those that received DHPCCB and hydralazine
(p=0.06).
CONCLUSIONS: Many patients in this cohort may not have
needed to receive acute antihypertensive therapy based on treat-
ment guidelines from the AHA. Labetalol resulted in a more pre-
dictable reduction of BP in the acute period. The largest
reductions in BP were seen with nitroprusside, hydralazine, and
clonidine. Agent select did not have an effect on patient outcome;
however, in patients who were treated outside the AHA guide-
lines a trend towards worse outcome was observed in patients
who received DHPCCB and hydralazine. Institutional treatment
guidelines are currently being developed.
POS.120
The Stiff Person Syndrome: A Single Case
Report of Almost Complete Recovery 12
Weeks following Immunomodulatory
Therapy with IVIG and Plasmapheresis
Catherine M. Dalton, Eetuan Lim, Janice Redmond, Dublin,
Ireland
OBJECTIVE: To institute an immunomodulatory treatment
that would arrest the respiratory spasms and reverse the stiffness
in a 36 year old lady with a four year history of progressive
stiffness who was diagnosed as having stiff person syndrome.
BACKGROUND: Stiff person syndrome is characterised by
stiffness, rigidity and spasm, due to impairment of inhibitory
pathways enhanced by GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) due to
an autoantibody against the CNS enzyme GAD (glutamic acid
decarboxylase). The patient was well until the birth of her baby
when she started complaining of stiffness, cramps, spasms, re-
stricted eye movement, dystonic posturing, hypertonicity, clonus,
hyper-reflexia and bilateral extensor plantar response. MRI brain

and cord were normal. Serum anti-GAD antibody was positive
consistent with stiff person syndrome. Over the previous six
months she had rapidly disimproved and required wheelchair,
PEG tube, tracheostomy, and bladder catheterisation.
DESIGN/METHODS: Five plasma exchanges with a total vol-
ume exchanged of 12,353 ml were given over 6 days. Intravenous
Immunoglobulin was given at a dose of 0.4 g/kg/day for five days.
RESULTS: Initially there was no response to either plasma
exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin. Twelve weeks later,
she demonstrated a marked improvement. She is now walking
unaided and completely independent in her activities of daily
living.
CONCLUSIONS: Stiff person syndrome is a rare, generally
progressive neurological disorder with impairment of descending
inhibitory pathways mediated by the inhibitory neurotransmitter
GABA due to anti-GAD antibodies. Delayed recovery 12-16 weeks
following IVIG and plasmapheresis is extremely rare. Trial of
IVIG and plasmapheresis is worth considering in patients with
stiff person syndrome whose disease is life threatening.
A376 NEUROLOGY 54 April 2000 (Suppl 3)
